complete_examples.text: Eq. (23) can be solved by the step-by-step time integration methods to obtain simultaneously the dynamic responses of the running vehicle and the guiding track structures.

Track irregularity probabilistic model aims at simulating representative and realistic track irregularity sets endowed with probabilities, and the vehicle/track coupled model is developed to obtain the dynamic responses of vehicle/track systems excited by track irregularities.

Then, from aspects of probability statistics and frequency analysis, an illustrative example is particularly conducted to comprehensively characterize the dynamic responses of vehicle–slab track systems, in which the representative and realistic rail irregularity sets simulated by the track irregularity probabilistic model are used as the loading inputs.

Until now, the significant work toward modeling vehicle–slab track interactions have been presented by many researchers, such as Lei and Wang (2014) and Yang et al. (2015) who presented the general vehicle–slab track FE models to investigate the dynamic responses of slab track systems.

The related work has been conducted by many researchers, for instance, Zhai and Sun [1,2] conducted pioneering work on parameters optimization to improve the wheel/rail dynamic interactions based on a vertical vehicle–track interaction model; Kaewunruen and Remennikov [3] presented an SA to analyze the free vibrations of an in situ concrete sleeper, in which the influence of variation of rail-pad parameters on the behavior of sleepers is identified, and similar works are presented in Refs. [4] and [5]; for assessing the effects of the inertial properties of railway vehicles on their dynamic responses, Suarez et al. [6] performed dynamic simulations accounting for the masses, moments of inertia, and heights of the center of gravity of the car body, bogie, and wheelset one at a time; Zakeri et al. [7] considered the coupled vertical and roll vibrations of a horizontally curved bridge to analyze the SA of the variables, e.g., cant, train speed, track quality, radius of curvature, etc.

However, one should realize a fact that though one or several track irregularity types form the most sensitive group to the dynamic responses of system components, the FOSI or the total sensitive index is varied against time, as shown in Figs. 5(a) and 6(a), due to the intrinsically time-varying amplitude–frequency characteristics of track irregularities.

Some conclusions are drawn from the results: (1) the largest dynamic responses of the coupled system for all items and cases are no longer changed when the vehicle number exceeds three, and three vehicles are adequate to guarantee the simulation precision to investigate the dynamic responses of the coupled system.

Yang et al. [10] studied the effects of random track irregularity and vehicle velocity on the dynamic responses of slab tracks using a vehicle-CRTS I slab track in a subgrade interaction model, in which composite track elements were used to rapidly model the slab track.

Moreover, the difference between the dynamic responses of the unit base plate and longitudinal connected base plate subject to different combination of wavelength and amplitude of soil deformation is analyzed.

Gou et al. [5] conducted a research on the mapping relationship between bridge deformation-induced geometric excitation and dynamic responses of high-speed trains (HST), and the threshold of pier settlement was obtained via mathematical derivation and numerical analysis [6].
